screens.title: Working with APIs and Data Persistence in React Native
screens.subtitle: Fetch remote data, render performant lists, and persist small state on device

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn how a typical React Native app talks to the network and saves small pieces of data on the device. We start with the built-in fetch A P I to retrieve JSON from a server, manage loading and error states so your UI never surprises people, and use FlatList or SectionList to render long data sets efficiently. Then we cover AsyncStorage for saving tiny bits of non-sensitive data, like a last searched city or a preference. You will see a concrete example that fetches posts from a public A P I, a small weather app workflow that persists the last city, and the key security rule: do not store secrets unencrypted. This knowledge matters because nearly every mobile app needs reliable network patterns and predictable persistence. By the end you'll know how to fetch, display, cache minimally, and avoid common pitfalls that break performance or leak data. Ready to explore practical code, common errors, and a simple persistence pattern you can reuse?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: Over the next screens you'll gain four practical competencies. First, you'll fetch data from remote APIs using the built-in fetch A P I and understand when axios might be preferable. I will show the mechanics of making requests, checking response status, and parsing JSON so you can avoid silent failures. Second, you'll display fetched data using FlatList or SectionList, and you'll learn the importance of keyExtractor and lazy rendering for performance. Third, you'll handle loading and error states: how to show ActivityIndicator during network calls and how to surface meaningful messages when a request fails. Finally, you'll persist small non-sensitive data with AsyncStorage, stringify objects before saving, and restore that data when your component mounts. Each objective includes a short mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can test that you can fetch, render, handle errors, and persist state reliably in a sample app.

screens.title: Fetching JSON with fetch and useEffect
screens.subtitle: A concrete example that retrieves posts and handles HTTP and network errors

narration.text: Let's walk through a practical fetch pattern you will use many times. The pattern uses useEffect to run once when a component mounts, and useState to hold posts, loading, and error values. Inside the effect we define an async function that calls fetch. Always check response. ok; a network response may succeed at the transport level while the server returns a 404 or 500. If response. ok is false, throw an Error to enter the catch block. In catch we set a user-friendly error and can optionally show an Alert for immediate feedback. Finally we set loading false in a finally block so the UI always leaves the loading state. A concrete example fetches posts from a public endpoint and stores them in state, which a FlatList can later render. A common misconception is to omit response. ok checks or to forget finalizing loading state on both success and failure; this creates infinite spinners or empty screens. Try this pattern and then change the URL to an invalid path to confirm your error flow shows an informative message. How will you signal network failures in your own app?

keyIdea.title: Fetch pattern
keyIdea.text: Use useEffect with an async fetch, check response.ok, parse JSON, set state, and always finalize loading in finally.

content.html:
Core Concept

Fetch with useEffect

This snippet shows the canonical pattern: fetch, validate response, parse JSON, handle errors, and update loading state so the UI remains predictable.

// App.js - fetch posts
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

export default function PostListScreen() {
  const [posts, setPosts] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const fetchPosts = async () => {
      try {
        const response = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts');
        if (!response.ok) {
          throw new Error(`HTTP error! status: ${response.status}`);
        }
        const json = await response.json();
        setPosts(json);
      } catch (e) {
        setError('Failed to load posts. Please try again later.');
      } finally {
        setLoading(false);
      }
    };
    fetchPosts();
  }, []);
}
Explanation & example
  • Define loading and error state so the UI can show an ActivityIndicator or an error message.
  • Check response.ok to catch HTTP errors rather than assuming success.
  • Use finally to ensure loading is cleared whether the call succeeds or fails.
Concrete example
Try the URL above; then change it to an invalid path to confirm your catch block runs and your ActivityIndicator stops.
Key Takeaway

Always validate responses and clear loading state so users see accurate feedback.

screens.title: Loading and Error States
screens.subtitle: Design a reliable UI that never leaves users guessing

narration.text: A polished networked app manages three primary UI states: loading, success, and error. Loading signals activity and prevents premature interaction; success displays the data and enables normal flow; error explains what went wrong and how to recover. Implementing this means setting a loading flag before a fetch, clearing it in finally, and populating either data or an error string. Use ActivityIndicator to communicate loading visually, and use inline messages or an Alert to show errors. A common mistake is only setting loading on the first request and forgetting to set it when the user triggers subsequent fetches, which results in stale UI. Also avoid swallowing errors silently in consoles; surface user-facing messages so the app remains usable. For a guided example, try fetching a city's weather: on submit set loading true, fetch, save successful city to AsyncStorage, and set loading false. If the fetch fails, show an error and allow retry. What retry strategy makes sense for your app? Loading and Error States means explicitly manage loading, success, and error states; always set loading before fetch and clear it in finally so ui stays consistent.. In practical terms, design a reliable ui that never leaves users guessing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UI states
keyIdea.text: Explicitly manage loading, success, and error states; always set loading before fetch and clear it in finally so UI stays consistent.

content.html:
Process Flow

Loading → Success → Error

1. Start fetch: setLoading(true), clear previous error.
2. Success: parse JSON, setData, optionally save to cache or AsyncStorage.
3. Error: set error message, show Alert or inline message, allow retry.
4. Finalize: in finally setLoading(false) so spinner stops.
Example UI elements
  • ActivityIndicator while loading to avoid blank screens.
  • Inline error text with a short retry button (or suggestion) when fetch fails.
  • Clear previous data when starting a new fetch to avoid confused displays.
Common Mistake

Leaving loading true on error leads to a never-ending spinner. Always clear loading in finally.

Key Takeaway

Explicit state transitions keep your UI predictable and prevent negative user experiences.

screens.title: fetch vs axios
screens.subtitle: When to rely on built-in fetch and when axios may help

narration.text: React Native includes a global fetch A P I that is promise-based and covers most basic HTTP needs. Fetch is simple and requires minimal dependency management, making it a good choice for straightforward GET requests and small apps. axios is a popular third-party library that adds conveniences such as automatic JSON parsing, request and response interceptors, and slightly more ergonomic error objects. If you need to centralize token refresh, add headers globally, or intercept responses for logging, axios' interceptors are valuable. However, axios is an added dependency, and many fetch features can be implemented manually with small wrappers. A typical approach is to start with fetch and extract common patterns into helper functions; move to axios only when features like interceptors or automatic transforms meaningfully reduce boilerplate. A common misconception is that axios is always faster; the choice is about developer ergonomics and features rather than raw performance. Decide based on your app's needs for interceptors, error handling shape, and team preferences. fetch vs axios means use fetch for simple needs. use axios when you need interceptors, global configuration, or richer error handling.. In practical terms, when to rely on built-in fetch and when axios may help. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tool choice
keyIdea.text: Use fetch for simple needs. Use axios when you need interceptors, global configuration, or richer error handling.

content.html:
Comparison
fetch (built-in)

Promise-based, no extra dependency. Good for basic GET/POST flows where you handle JSON parsing and errors manually.

axios (third-party)

Provides interceptors, automatic transforms, and consistent error objects. Useful for token refresh or global request config.

Decision guide
  1. Start with fetch for small apps and simple requests.
  2. Use axios when interceptors and global configuration reduce duplication.
  3. If you need fine-grained error shapes, axios often gives clearer error objects.
Key Takeaway

Choose tools for features you need, not for perceived speed differences.

screens.title: FlatList and SectionList
screens.subtitle: How virtualization keeps long lists performant

narration.text: FlatList and SectionList are React Native components designed to render large lists efficiently by virtualizing off-screen items. Virtualization means the list only creates components for items currently visible plus a small buffer, instead of rendering the entire dataset into memory. For FlatList you supply data array, renderItem and a keyExtractor function that returns a stable key such as item. id. toString(). SectionList is similar but organizes items into grouped sections with titles and data arrays for each section. A common mistake is using ScrollView for long datasets; ScrollView renders all children at once and will likely cause slow rendering and memory issues. When using FlatList, avoid inline functions that recreate item components unnecessarily, memoize renderItem when possible, and provide a stable keyExtractor to prevent re-render churn. For lists with heterogeneous rows consider getItemLayout for fixed-height rows to improve scroll performance. How many items will your app need to handle before virtualized lists are essential? FlatList and SectionList means flatlist and sectionlist render only visible items, reducing memory and improving scroll performance for long lists.. In practical terms, how virtualization keeps long lists performant. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: List virtualization
keyIdea.text: FlatList and SectionList render only visible items, reducing memory and improving scroll performance for long lists.

content.html:
Definition

Virtualized lists

FlatList takes props: data, renderItem, keyExtractor. It renders items lazily as they become visible.

SectionList groups data into sections with titles and individual data arrays per section, useful for categorized lists.

Practical tips
  • Provide keyExtractor that returns a string, e.g., item.id.toString().
  • Memoize renderItem or use PureComponent for item rows to reduce re-renders.
  • Use getItemLayout when row height is fixed to speed up initial scroll.
Common Mistake

Using ScrollView for large datasets leads to poor performance. Prefer FlatList for long or unknown-length lists.

screens.title: AsyncStorage basics
screens.subtitle: Simple, asynchronous key-value persistence for non-sensitive data

narration.text: AsyncStorage is a lightweight key-value store for React Native intended for small, non-sensitive data like user preferences or a cached response. It stores strings asynchronously, so before saving complex values you must JSON. stringify them; when reading, parse the string back to an object. Use AsyncStorage. setItem(key, value) and AsyncStorage. getItem(key) which return Promises; wrap them in try... catch to handle possible failures. Because AsyncStorage is unencrypted, do not store passwords, tokens, or financial data there—secure storage solutions are required for secrets. A simple flow is: on successful A P I fetch save the item, and on app mount load the last saved value and use it to seed your component state. A common misconception is treating AsyncStorage as instantaneous synchronous storage; because it returns Promises, the UI must await or handle loading while values are read. Test persistence by restarting the app and verifying values are restored. AsyncStorage basics means asynchronous string-based key-value storage. stringify objects before saving and avoid storing sensitive information.. In practical terms, simple, asynchronous key-value persistence for non-sensitive data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: AsyncStorage
keyIdea.text: Asynchronous string-based key-value storage. Stringify objects before saving and avoid storing sensitive information.

content.html:
Definition

What is AsyncStorage?

A simple, unencrypted, asynchronous key-value storage mechanism for small amounts of non-sensitive data in React Native.

API snippets
import AsyncStorage from '@react-native-async-storage/async-storage';

await AsyncStorage.setItem('last_city', JSON.stringify('London'));
const stored = await AsyncStorage.getItem('last_city');
const city = stored ? JSON.parse(stored) : null;
Practical guidance
  • Always JSON.stringify before saving non-string values.
  • Await getItem on mount and initialize component state from the value.
  • Do not store secrets. Use a secure storage plugin for sensitive tokens.
Example

Save the last searched city after a successful weather fetch so the app can load it automatically on next launch.

screens.title: Weather app: fetch, show loading, persist last city
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step starter that ties fetch, loading, and AsyncStorage together

narration.text: Let's combine the ideas into a simple weather app flow you can build. Start with a default city state and an input where the user types a city name. On submit set loading true and clear previous errors. Call fetch with the city name; if response. ok parse the JSON and set weatherData; then call AsyncStorage. setItem('last_searched_city', cityName) so the app remembers it. In the component's useEffect, attempt to load last_searched_city from AsyncStorage and, if present, set city state and trigger a fetch for that city. Always wrap storage and network calls in try... catch to surface failures. This flow teaches two core behaviors: how to seed UI state from persisted values and how to save successful user choices for future sessions. A misconception to avoid is saving the search term before confirming a successful fetch; save only after you have valid results so you don't persist invalid or misspelled entries. keyIdea.title: Weather flow
keyIdea.text: On search, fetch weather, save successful city to AsyncStorage, and load saved city on mount to restore the last session.

content.html:
Process Flow

Search → Fetch → Save → Restore

// key parts of the flow
// load last city on mount
useEffect(() => {
  const loadLastCity = async () => {
    try {
      const storedCity = await AsyncStorage.getItem('last_searched_city');
      if (storedCity) setCity(storedCity);
    } catch (e) { console.error('Failed to load last city:', e); }
  };
  loadLastCity();
}, []);

// on search
const handleSearch = async () => {
  setLoading(true); setError(null);
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`https://api.example/weather?q=${city}&appid=KEY&units=metric`);
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error('City not found');
    const data = await response.json();
    setWeatherData(data);
    await AsyncStorage.setItem('last_searched_city', city);
  } catch (e) {
    setError(e.message || 'Failed to fetch weather.');
  } finally {
    setLoading(false);
  }
};
Notes & best practices
  • Save the city only after a successful fetch to avoid persisting invalid data.
  • Handle invalid responses (404) with a clear message and let the user retry.
  • Use ActivityIndicator while loading and disable inputs to prevent duplicate requests.
Key Takeaway

Seed state from storage on mount and update storage only on confirmed success to keep persisted data meaningful.

screens.title: Rendering posts with FlatList
screens.subtitle: Concrete FlatList example with keyExtractor and item row considerations

narration.text: Now let's render the posts we fetched using FlatList. Provide the data array, a renderItem function that returns a compact view for each post, and a keyExtractor that returns a string key such as item. id. toString(). Keeping each row small and focused helps the virtualization system. Avoid heavy layout work inside renderItem like complex images or unbounded text; instead prefer compact previews and navigation into a detail screen for larger content. Memoize item rows or use React. memo to avoid repeated renders for unchanged items. A common misconception is that keyExtractor is optional; without unique stable keys React will re-render more often which harms performance. In our example each post row shows title and body excerpt, allowing FlatList to efficiently measure and render only visible rows. Consider showing a separator and a simple onPress to navigate to a full post view if your app requires deeper interaction. screens.title: Saving and loading JSON with AsyncStorage
screens.subtitle: How to stringify, save, retrieve, and parse values safely

narration.text: Saving structured data requires converting it to a string because AsyncStorage stores strings only. Use JSON. stringify for objects and JSON. parse when reading. Wrap both operations in try... catch because serialization or storage errors can occur, especially on low-disk devices. Save only after you have valid data; for example, after a successful weather fetch save the city name or the cached response you want to reuse. When loading on mount, treat the result as possibly null and handle that case gracefully by using defaults. A subtle mistake developers make is assuming getItem always returns a value; it may return null, so check and avoid parsing null directly. For larger or sensitive datasets, migrate to encrypted storage or a database. Practice by saving a small preferences object and confirming persistence by reloading the app. What default should your UI show while storage is loading? Saving and loading JSON with AsyncStorage means json.stringify values before setitem and json.parse after getitem; handle null returns and wrap operations in try...catch.. In practical terms, how to stringify, save, retrieve, and parse values safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Stringify & parse
keyIdea.text: JSON.stringify values before setItem and JSON.parse after getItem; handle null returns and wrap operations in try...catch.

content.html:
Process Flow

Save → Load

Save: const json = JSON.stringify(value); await AsyncStorage.setItem(key, json);

Load: const raw = await AsyncStorage.getItem(key); const value = raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : null;

Always guard parse with try...catch to avoid corrupt data crashes.

Example scenario
After a successful weather fetch, save { lastCity: 'London' } as JSON so the app can automatically fetch for that city on next launch.
Common Mistake

Parsing null without checking leads to exceptions. Always check the returned string before JSON.parse.

screens.title: Security considerations for persistence
screens.subtitle: What is safe to store in AsyncStorage and what is not

narration.text: AsyncStorage is convenient but unencrypted. Use it for small, non-sensitive data like UI preferences, the last searched city, or cached non-sensitive responses. Do not store passwords, refresh tokens, or financial data in AsyncStorage; these require secure, encrypted storage such as platform secure storage or specialized libraries. Another security pitfall is storing raw tokens without expiry handling; if tokens are compromised, the app should be able to revoke them server-side and remove them locally. When in doubt, prefer short-lived server-side tokens and refresh them securely, or use appropriate secure storage packages that encrypt on device. A practical test is to try reading AsyncStorage contents from a rooted emulator to understand how unprotected the storage may be. The goal is to balance convenience for non-sensitive persistence with strong protection for anything that could lead to account compromise. Security considerations for persistence means use asyncstorage only for non-sensitive data. use encrypted platform storage for secrets, tokens, and financial information.. In practical terms, what is safe to store in asyncstorage and what is not. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Security rule
keyIdea.text: Use AsyncStorage only for non-sensitive data. Use encrypted platform storage for secrets, tokens, and financial information.

content.html:
Definition

What to store in AsyncStorage

  • Safe: UI theme, last searched city, non-sensitive caches.
  • Unsafe: passwords, refresh tokens, credit card data.
  • Alternative: use secure storage or encrypted databases for sensitive items.
Best practices
  1. Never persist secrets in plaintext.
  2. Prefer short-lived tokens and server-side validation.
  3. Remove persisted tokens on logout and rotate credentials appropriately.
Key Takeaway

AsyncStorage is great for convenience, not for secrets. Choose encrypted storage when security matters.

screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging tips
screens.subtitle: Practical checks for common issues when working with APIs and storage

narration.text: Here are common pitfalls and how to debug them. First, if your UI shows an endless spinner, confirm you set loading false in finally and that your catch block doesn't swallow the state update. Second, if FlatList re-renders unexpectedly, ensure keyExtractor returns stable keys and that renderItem is memoized or not recreated each render. Third, if your persisted data seems missing after an app restart, check for typos in keys and confirm setItem succeeded; always await setItem and handle errors. For network failures inspect response. ok and log response. status; do not assume fetch throws on 404. When debugging, reproduce the failure by changing the URL or simulating a network error and then trace the state transitions in console logs. Finally, test persistence by restarting the simulator to confirm the load flow. After you fix bugs, consider writing small smoke tests to ensure essential flows—fetch, render, save, load—work end to end. Common mistakes and debugging tips means ensure loading is always cleared, keys are stable for lists, await asyncstorage operations, and check response.ok for http errors.. In practical terms, practical checks for common issues when working with apis and storage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Debug checklist
keyIdea.text: Ensure loading is always cleared, keys are stable for lists, await AsyncStorage operations, and check response.ok for HTTP errors.

content.html:
Checklist
  • Loading stuck? Ensure setLoading(false) in finally.
  • FlatList jitter? Use stable keys and memoized rows.
  • Missing persisted data? Await setItem and check keys spelling.
  • Silent API errors? Check response.ok and inspect status codes.
Debugging tips

Simulate network failures by changing endpoints or toggling network mode in your emulator. Add console logs around state updates to verify transitions. Test persistence by restarting the app and verifying load paths.

Key Takeaway

Use targeted simulations to reproduce failures and verify each state change in your network and storage flows.

screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important concepts you should remember. First, fetch is built-in and promise-based; always check response. ok and parse JSON safely. Second, FlatList and SectionList virtualize long lists, so supply data, renderItem, and a stable keyExtractor to keep scrolling smooth. Third, AsyncStorage stores strings only, so stringify objects and never store sensitive data there. These three pillars—reliable fetching, efficient rendering, and cautious persistence—form the practical foundation for many mobile features. As you build, apply small tests: change endpoints to exercise error handling, populate long lists to test FlatList performance, and restart the app to confirm AsyncStorage persistence. Keeping these rules in mind will make your apps feel robust and predictable. screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to reuse in your projects

narration.text: Keep three compact rules at your fingertips. Rule one: always validate HTTP responses and handle errors visibly so users understand network problems. Rule two: use FlatList or SectionList rather than ScrollView for long lists and provide stable keys to minimize re-renders. Rule three: use AsyncStorage for convenience but never for secrets—stringify objects and prefer secure storage for tokens. These practical rules reduce bugs, protect users, and keep apps fast. When you start a new feature that touches network or persistence, run a short checklist: response. ok handled, loader shown, error surfaced, keys stable, and persisted values verified after restart. This routine will save debugging time and protect user data in small but meaningful ways. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Key Concepts
Handle HTTP errors
Check response.ok, show clear errors, and always clear loading state.
Virtualize lists
Use FlatList/SectionList with a stable keyExtractor to preserve performance.
Safe persistence
AsyncStorage is unencrypted. Use it for preferences only; encrypt secrets elsewhere.
One-line takeaway

Reliable apps validate network responses, render lists efficiently, and protect users by keeping sensitive data out of unencrypted storage.

ai_generation_note:
Create a 15-minute live coding video. Begin by setting up a component to fetch data from `jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts` using `fetch` within `useEffect`. Show how to handle loading states with `ActivityIndicator` and basic error handling with `Alert`. Then, integrate `FlatList` to render the fetched posts, explaining `data`, `renderItem`, and `keyExtractor`. Next, demonstrate `AsyncStorage`: install the package, then add functionality to save and load a simple user preference (e.g., a "favorite color" string) using `AsyncStorage.setItem` and `AsyncStorage.getItem`. Show how to test persistence by restarting the app (e.g., by closing and reopening the emulator). Emphasize security warnings for `AsyncStorage`.
